# The idea {.unnumbered}

## What this note assumes

This note assumes familiarity with the ordinary nonparametric bootstrap and
Dirichlet-distributed probability vectors. Read the
[Dirac measure note](../Measure_Theory/dirac-measure-and-dirac-delta.qmd) and
[KL divergence](../Other/km-divergence.qmd) first. The
[Bayesian measure-notation guide](bayes-measure-d-concept.qmd) explains
$\Pi(dF\mid X_{1:n})$. No advanced measure theory is otherwise assumed.

Given observed values $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the Bayesian bootstrap represents
uncertainty about their population probabilities by assigning random weights
[@rubin1981bayesianbootstrap]. A posterior draw is the probability measure

$$
F^{(b)}=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}\delta_{X_i},
\qquad
(W_1^{(b)},\ldots,W_n^{(b)})
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,\ldots,1).
\tag{1}
$$

The notation in (1) matters:

- $F^{(b)}$ is a probability measure;
- $\delta_{X_i}$ is a Dirac point mass;
- $F^{(b)}$ is not an ordinary density relative to Lebesgue measure.

Dirichlet$(1,\ldots,1)$ is a continuous distribution over every nonnegative
weight vector whose entries sum to one. With all parameters equal to one, it
is uniform over that simplex; it is a modeling choice, not a consequence of
measure notation.

The **simplex** is just the set of all such weight vectors. It is a line
segment for two weights, a filled triangle for three, and the analogous
higher-dimensional shape for more weights.

# The random object {#bootstrap-random-object}

The observations are fixed after being observed. The weights are random:

$$
W_i\geq0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^nW_i=1.
$$

Every weight draw gives an entire distribution supported on the observed data.
The induced law of $F$ is the Bayesian-bootstrap posterior
$\Pi(dF\mid X_{1:n})$.

For a measurable function $h$,

$$
\int h(x)F^{(b)}(dx)
=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}h(X_i).
\tag{2}
$$

Equation (2) converts a distributional functional into a random weighted
statistic.

A **functional** is a rule whose input is an entire distribution. For example,
the mean, median, variance, or a regression coefficient defined by an
estimating equation can all be written as $T(F)$.

# Repeated observed values

If the distinct observed values are $x_1^*,\ldots,x_K^*$ with counts
$n_1,\ldots,n_K$, the equivalent combined representation is

$$
F^{(b)}=\sum_{k=1}^KV_k^{(b)}\delta_{x_k^*},
\qquad
(V_1^{(b)},\ldots,V_K^{(b)})
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(n_1,\ldots,n_K).
$$

This follows because sums of components of a Dirichlet vector are again
Dirichlet with the corresponding parameters added.

# Posterior mean distribution

Because $E(W_i)=1/n$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar F_n(A)
&=E\{F^{(b)}(A)\mid X_{1:n}\}\\
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1(X_i\in A).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the posterior mean measure is the empirical distribution

$$
\widehat F_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}.
\tag{3}
$$

# Obtaining a posterior for a functional

Suppose the estimand is a functional $T(F)$, such as a mean, quantile, risk
difference, or a parameter defined by an estimating equation. The algorithm is

1. draw $W^{(b)}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,\ldots,1)$;
2. construct $F^{(b)}$ through (1);
3. compute $T^{(b)}=T(F^{(b)})$;
4. repeat to approximate the posterior distribution of $T(F)$.

For the mean,

$$
T^{(b)}=\int xF^{(b)}(dx)
=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}X_i.
$$

For a population estimating equation

$$
\int\psi(x,\theta)F(dx)=0,
$$

each draw solves

$$
\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}\psi(X_i,\theta^{(b)})=0.
$$

# Frequentist bootstrap comparison

For one ordinary nonparametric-bootstrap resample,

$$
\widehat F_n^*
=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{N_i}{n}\delta_{X_i},
\qquad
(N_1,\ldots,N_n)
\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}
\left(n;\frac1n,\ldots,\frac1n\right).
$$

| Feature | Ordinary bootstrap | Bayesian bootstrap |
|---|---|---|
| Random weights | $N_i/n$, discrete multiples of $1/n$ | $W_i$, continuous Dirichlet weights |
| Main interpretation | Approximate repeated-sampling distribution | Posterior uncertainty under the Bayesian-bootstrap model |
| Resampled dataset | Yes, explicitly or through counts | No; random probability weights |
| Support | Observed values | Observed values |

The two procedures can yield similar computations but have different
inferential interpretations.

# What assumptions are and are not being made

Exchangeability helps motivate treating labels symmetrically, but
exchangeability **alone** does not imply Dirichlet$(1,\ldots,1)$ weights. The
Dirichlet law is an additional Bayesian-bootstrap modeling choice.

Exchangeability here means that relabeling observations does not change the
joint probability model. It expresses label symmetry, not independence and
not a unique prior distribution.

The Bayesian bootstrap also places posterior mass only on distributions
supported by observed values. Consequently, under the basic construction it
assigns no predictive probability to a genuinely new support point. This can
be reasonable for functionals of an unknown distribution but is not an
innocuous model for every scientific problem.

“Supported by observed values” means every posterior draw assigns probability
one to the finite set $\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}$. Any point outside that set receives
probability zero.

# Walker's decision-theory calculation {#bootstrap-walker-decision}

Let $f_\theta$ be a parametric density used as an action, and score it by
negative KL divergence from $F$ to $P_\theta$. For a Bayesian-bootstrap draw,
the part of the utility that depends on $\theta$ is

$$
\int\log f_\theta(x)F^{(b)}(dx)
=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}\log f_\theta(X_i).
\tag{4}
$$

## Collapsing uncertainty first

If we maximize expected posterior utility, replace $F^{(b)}$ by its posterior
mean (3):

$$
\int\log f_\theta(x)\widehat F_n(dx)
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log f_\theta(X_i).
$$

The maximizer is the ordinary maximum likelihood estimator.

## Preserving the full posterior uncertainty

Alternatively, for each Dirichlet draw solve

$$
\theta^{(b)}
=\arg\max_\theta
\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}\log f_\theta(X_i).
\tag{5}
$$

The empirical distribution of the $\theta^{(b)}$ values propagates uncertainty
from the random $F$. Walker connects (5) to the weighted likelihood bootstrap
of Newton and Raftery [@newton1994weighted].

Expected utility and draw-by-draw decisions answer different questions:

- expected utility produces one Bayes action;
- draw-by-draw optimization induces a distribution over projected parametric
  actions.

# Common mistakes

1. Writing $f(x)=\sum_iW_i\delta_{X_i}(x)$ and calling it a Lebesgue density.
   Use the measure $F=\sum_iW_i\delta_{X_i}$.
2. Saying the Dirichlet weights follow from exchangeability alone.
3. Forgetting to combine weights when observed values repeat.
4. Claiming the Bayesian bootstrap estimates the full smooth data-generating
   density. Its draws remain supported on observed values.
5. Treating the ordinary and Bayesian bootstrap as identical because both use
   random weights.

# Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. What type of object is $F^{(b)}$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$F^{(b)}=\sum_iW_i^{(b)}\delta_{X_i}$ is a discrete probability measure on
the observation space. It assigns mass $W_i^{(b)}$ to observed point $X_i$
(with masses added when values repeat). It is not a Lebesgue density.
:::

**2. Why is its posterior mean the empirical distribution?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

For Dirichlet$(1,\ldots,1)$ weights, $E(W_i^{(b)})=1/n$. Therefore, for every
measurable $A$,

$$
E\{F^{(b)}(A)\mid X_{1:n}\}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1(X_i\in A),
$$

which is exactly the empirical measure
$\widehat F_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$.
:::

**3. What changes when observations contain ties?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Weights attached to equal observed values are combined. If the distinct values
$x_1^*,\ldots,x_K^*$ have counts $n_1,\ldots,n_K$, then

$$
F^{(b)}=\sum_{k=1}^KV_k^{(b)}\delta_{x_k^*},
\qquad
(V_1^{(b)},\ldots,V_K^{(b)})
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(n_1,\ldots,n_K).
$$
:::

**4. Which choice produces the MLE: maximizing under each draw or maximizing
posterior expected utility?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Maximizing **posterior expected utility** replaces $F^{(b)}$ by its posterior
mean $\widehat F_n$ and maximizes
$n^{-1}\sum_i\log f_\theta(X_i)$, so it produces the ordinary MLE. Maximizing
separately under every draw instead produces many randomly weighted estimates
$\theta^{(b)}$, a distribution of projected actions.
:::

**5. What modeling restriction follows from support only on observed points?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Every basic Bayesian-bootstrap posterior draw assigns probability one to
$\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}$. It assigns zero probability to every genuinely new
support point. This can be suitable for uncertainty about functionals but is a
strong restriction if prediction at unseen values or smooth density estimation
is the scientific goal.
:::
